#1090. Much-improved Newcastle stop the rot with a 1-1 draw at Fulham - but 'slapstick' defending and wasteful finishing will leave Matthias Jaissle rueing a missed opportunity, writes CRAIG HOPE

Published: 12:52 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 19:24 EDT, 7 November 2026

Just when Newcastle looked set for victory after Jacob Murphy had borrowed Amar Dedic's bow to arrow them into a late lead, they turned the weapon on themselves.

After a week in which Dedic, Bosnia's answer to Robin Hood, had made headlines when pursued by police for wandering around the Northumberland countryside with his hunting gear, the Geordies were ready to rob the good folk of west London after Murphy found the target ten minutes from time.

Less than three minutes later and they were picking the arrow from their own foot. William Osula failed to protect possession and allowed Fulham to enter the penalty area. Then, with the ball bouncing around the goalmouth, it was home substitute Rodrigo Muniz who pounced to punish Newcastle's scruffy defending.

'Slapstick', visiting boss Matthias Jaissle later called it.

The German also said that his team deserved to win but you got the impression he was relieved to emerge without defeat, especially as the performance was improved on the back of a run of four losses in five.

Newcastle's second-half spirit also showed a response to a week of noise centred on dressing-room unrest, not to mention Dedic's police drama.

Jacob Murphy thought he had won it for Newcastle after scoring late on at Craven Cottage

Rodrigo Muniz netted moments later after sloppy defending from Newcastle, earning a 1-1 draw

Matthias Jaissle's side were much improved but must cut out the errors to win matches

And Jaissle was right in that his team could have left with three points had master archer Harvey Barnes not missed a hat-trick of chances.

Fulham (4-2-3-1): Leno 7; Castagne 6 (Tete 77, 5), Affengruber 6, Bassey 6, Robinson 5; Berge 6, Charles 6; Bobb 6 (Sessegnon 78, 6), King 7 (Palacios 72, 5), Iwobi 6; Garcia 4 (Muniz 65, 8)

Subs not used: Lecomte, Andersen, Hugo Larsson, Manuel Angel, Kevin

Newcastle (4-2-3-1): Hornicek 7; Dedic 6, Thiaw 7 (Schar 85, 6), Burn 7, Hall 6; Nico Gonzalez 5 (Miley 61, 6), Steur 7 (Fernandez-Pardo 74, 5); Murphy 8, Wissa 6 (Willock 61, 5), Barnes 6; Osula 5 (Elanga 85)

Subs not used: Pope, Livramento, Botman, Bazoumana Toure

The winger is the player to whom they'd want those opportunities to fall, too. But twice before half-time, when denied by Bernd Leno from close range, and then again when lashing wide after the break, he failed to give his side the advantage.

Murphy corrected his team-mate's finishing when capitalising on a loose pass from Cesar Palacios and slamming into the bottom corner from 25 yards, but that joy was short-lived.

In truth, there hadn't been much joy to behold all afternoon. The draw keeps both sides in the bottom half of the table, and that is where they will likely stay.

The first half, in particular, had very strong last-on-Match-of-the-Day vibes.

Newcastle thought they had a 33rd-minute lead when Dan Burn stole in at the near post to flick home from Murphy's low cross.

What the officials had spotted at the far post was linebacker Yoane Wissa pinning defender Timothy Castagne, and so playing Burn onside. It was the right call, even if Jaissle disagreed

'I learned that word here, a 'soft' decision. In my eyes, it was not right,' he said. 'But I was pleased with our complete commitment and togetherness.

'We grew through the game and that was excellent, something to build on. We showed the fundamentals.'

Dedic twice came close to creating goals with teasing crosses from the right, and you wondered if he would have mimicked Barnes' trademark archer celebration had they been converted.

He was kept away from the media post-match, but Jaissle did say: 'He played well, right? It (the bow & arrow incident) didn't affect him. He was not aware of the rules. We don't need to make a big deal out of it.'

Fulham's Josh King was included in Thomas Tuchel's England squad on Friday, the club's first Three Lions call-up in eight years. He, however, now needs a scan on a tight groin before learning if he's fit enough to feature.

Did the 19-year-old play like a would-be England international? He was his side's best player in the first half, even if that was a low bar to hurdle. One volley would have raised the roof had it gone in, so sweet was the connection from 20 yards. Lukas Hornicek needed every inch of his 6ft 6in frame to dive and save. And that, too, was a recurring theme, Newcastle's reliance on the big Czech to bail them out when giving up chances.

Like Newcastle, however, Fulham simply weren't good enough to take them.

#1089. Man Utd show fight on night of chaos to give Carrick a glimpse of hope

So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

And then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they were supposed to be and what they were supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club have served up some famous comebacks over the decades, but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

And yet by the 86th minute Matheus Cunha’s wild celebrations were encapsulating a wild night, the Brazilian ripping off his shirt after his dramatic winner before launching himself into a delirious crowd drunk on the euphoria of a victory that had seemed improbable in the extreme at the interval, when boos cascaded from the stands.

Whether this proves little more than a thrilling, heroic interlude in the endgame for Carrick, or the start of a genuine turnaround, is hard to know. And, let’s be clear, there was so much about the first-half performance to concern the hierarchy, who came under persistent, furious attack from fans at war with an ownership it reviles and wants gone.

But the second half stood firmly at odds with the shambolic display that had preceded it and suggested all may not be quite lost just yet.

Aston Villa visit Old Trafford on Sunday in the final game before the international break and, if Carrick can follow this with another win, then it will be intriguing to see where the Old Trafford board goes from there.

Carrick may at least have been encouraged by some of the things Bruno Fernandes said after the game, not least that he warranted being dropped against Bournemouth. And it was the captain who kick-started the fightback against Roma, albeit at the second attempt.

He had won the penalty after being fouled by Gianluca Mancini only to then contrive to miss it. But a retake was ordered for encroachment and, given a second bite at the cherry, Fernandes made no mistake.

NO MISTAKE THIS TIME 💪 Bruno Fernandes gets United back in it after a penalty retake 😤 https://t.co/uQdkNs0lXo

When Carlos Baleba pulled up with a hamstring injury within seconds of the restart as he burst into the penalty area, Carrick must have wondered what else could go wrong.

But as United went hell for leather, the home supporters who had spent much of the first half attacking the owners and staging a number of colourful protest acts, suddenly found their voice in a very different way.

From being an atmosphere in which the players clearly felt cowed, Old Trafford was now rallying behind its men in red – and it helped to shake Roma in the process. They had been such good value for their lead, but now they were rocking, and United smelled blood.

There was wave after wave of attack as Roma desperately and often frantically tried to defend their goal, and it took a bad mistake from Leonardo Balerdi, who swung at thin air from Fernandes’s cross and missed the ball, to hand Cunha the chance to equalise.

It was Lacey who speared an inch-perfect pass into Cunha, who turned sharply before drilling a stunning finish in off the near post. Cue bedlam.

When the clock hit 20.05 – a nod to the year 2005 when the Glazers bought the club – a pile of tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch from the Stretford End amid chants of “We Want Glazers Out”. They were quickly followed by cries of “Just like the Glazers, Jim Ratcliffe’s a c---” and “sell the club and f--- off home”.

Jason Wilcox, the club’s director of football, again copped for it. A banner read: “For the love, not the ‘likes’”. When the Champions League music played, hundreds of green and gold balloons – a reference to the club’s original colours and the 2010 protest movement – were released.

On the pitch, United were all over the place. At that point, no one could have reckoned on the comeback that followed. Where it leads, who knows.

Speaking after the match, Michael Carrick was very positive about his side’s performance.

“It was a good night. I have to a lot of credit to the players for starters, showing that character and that quality when we needed it and to the supporters. This place does incredible, magical things,” said Carrick.

“I thought we grew into it the first half  after giving the goals too easily. We spoke at half time about how this place can change, it only takes one moment and it certainly did that and the boys made the most of every opportunity and were fantastic in the end.”

Asked about how he inspired the team at half-time he kept it simple: “Just not to get too disappointed about things. I thought we were coming into the game, getting around their box and it didn’t feel that way to the players because they were carrying too much frustration and disappointment and I knew we were doing some good things in the game against a really good team.

“Playing against man-to-man as much as they are, you probably get more failure than success and it’s still being positive and the boys responded so well to that.”

As for whether this will change United’s momentum now, he was cautious not to get carried away.

“Listen it’s one game. It depends on what happens next and we’ve got to capitalise on that but tonight the boys showed an awful lot,” he said.

“And I thought we came out the second half, unfortunately with Carlos having to go off and Youri coming on the pitch and I thought he was fantastic, he showed everything that he is as a personality, as a character and with his experience to step in the game like that, and the boys just went with the flow and you could feel how positive it was and it was nice to see this place like that again.”

Captain Bruno Fernandes also spoke after the match, acknowledging the difficulties the team has faced.

“It’s tough to say something at the moment to be honest. It’s been a tough period for us, we have not been able to play in the way we want, get the results we want. We’ve done some good bits, but not had the consistency to do it through a whole game to get results and it’s been tough.

“But today was important to get a win. We knew after that we still had the fans with us, we felt we could change it with a goal and something and fortunately we did it today.”

As for his penalty miss and re-take: “First one didn’t go the way I wanted, I did something wrong but I got a second chance and I cleared my head and my mind was only on to get the ball in back of the net.

“It’s been tough for the fans, we understand that. Having that belief from their side helps the team a lot and today was one of those days that Old Trafford came alive.”

After his first start as he returns from injury, Kobbie Mainoo was full of praise for the fans, saying he cherished the relationship the team had with them.

“It’s unlike anything else. We’d do anything for these fans on the pitch, all the love they give us throughout the season it’s only right we repay them and it’s a bit of fun just jumping into the stands with them.”

Speaking to Amazon after the match, Youri Tielemans said: “There has been a lot of pressure on him [Carrick] and that’s how we repay him, with a comeback like this, big character, big fight.”

“We just kept working, we kept believing. We were on the front foot in the second half, we tried to push them into their goal and we succeeded.”

As for whether or not the performance would be enough to keep Carrick in his role at United: “That’s a different question. The only thing we can do is stick behind him, fight for him and fight for the club.

“At the end of the day we are on the pitch and we need to show what we are capable of and tonight, especially in the second half, we showed what we can do and we turned up the gears.

“Let’s hope this is a good turnaround for us and let’s hope we can build on this.”

Manchester United fans are planning a series of in-stadium demonstrations at Old Trafford tonight in protest at the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s ownership.

Thousands of green and gold balloons – a nod to the club’s original colours as Newton Heath – are set to be released from the Stretford End when the Champions League music plays out ahead of kick-off.

There had been plans to bring a banner into the stadium bearing the words: “No new stadium, we want new owners” but that was blocked, apparently on the grounds of Uefa’s inability to sanction it in time.

The Glazers and Ratcliffe have come under growing attack this season with the club’s regular match going supporters at war with the owners.

A separate fans’ group has also been encouraging fans to join in anti Glazers and Ratcliffe chants in the 21st minute or, more specifically, after 20 minutes and 5 seconds: 20.05 is a nod to 2005, the year the Glazers completed their hostile takeover at Old Trafford.

It’s matchday four of the Champions League and Michael Carrick’s side host their Serie A opponents having failed to win any of their last nine matches across all competitions. Since their win against Sabah back in September (must feel like years ago to Carrick), they have suffered chastening defeats in Europe to Atlético Madrid and then Cesc Fabregas’s Como. This has been coupled with dismal performances in the Premier League, most recently a 2-0 defeat at the hands of Chelsea, where Lisandro Martínez was sent off for two ridiculous fouls.

All in all, there is the feeling that Carrick is simply a dead man walking, limping towards the international break after the United hierarchy decided on a stay of execution in their crisis talks earlier this month. If the beleaguered manager has any hope at all of hanging on to his job, he needs convincing results tonight and against Aston Villa on the weekend.

Despite the doom-mongering that circles the club, Carrick maintains that he has buried the hatchet with Bruno Fernandes following his captain’s public criticisms of the club, insisting that “the dressing room is a good place” in his pre-match press conference (more on that to come).

The visitors on the other hand, managed by Gian Piero Gasperini – who replaced Claudio Ranieri last summer – are certainly having a better time of it. They got off to a slow start in Europe, drawing with Fernebahce in their opening match but coming agonisingly close to stunning Real Madrid on matchday two at home. They went 3-1 up before three late goals snatched victory for Madrid.

They bounced back with a convincing 4-0 win over Slovan Bratislava and their domestic campaign is off to an incredibly promising start. They are currently unbeaten in Serie A with seven wins and three draws. They sit third and are the highest scoring side, with 28 goals from their 10 games. #1088. Gianluigi Donnarumma was signed to be world's best shot-stopper, but at Manchester City, he's merely fine

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Hard as it may be to believe or justify after events in Leipzig, there was a logic to Manchester City jettisoning their decade-long policy for goalkeeper recruitment last summer and signing Gianluigi Donnarumma. When your greatest defensive attribute is how your possession constricts your opponents from your third of the pitch then what you want from your No.1 is someone who can keep and progress the ball. Ederson is the dream. Even an aged Claudio Bravo is tolerable.

That all changed when Rodri's anterior cruciate ligament went in September 2024. Suddenly Manchester City were unable to shut down the opposition, to block off the counter and keep the other team to hitting and hoping. Having allowed somewhere around seven and a half shots in each of the previous four seasons, City allowed 9.34 in 2024-25, 9.71 in 2025-26. Now that Enzo Maresca has taken the helm and concluded that Elliot Anderson is enough of a midfield, we are at 10.56 in the Premier League. In the Champions League, where so many of City's opponents know best how to play on the front foot, it is 11 shots allowed per game (that average isn't as warped by playing PSG as you think).

If you're going to allow that much extra pressure on your goal, you want someone who can keep the ball out. In principle, Gianluigi Donnarumma is that guy, certainly if he is the player who carried Paris Saint-Germain through so many crucial moments and to their first Champions League title. But, of course, he isn't.

In Leipzig tonight, the outfield players managed to cover for their increasingly error-prone goalkeeper, Erling Haaland scoring a 13th goal in nine meetings with the Bundesliga side and earning a 3-2 win for City. Covering for Donnarumma was not something this team were able to do when he let Nicolas Jackson's shot through his gloves at Villa Park, nor when he got done by Desire Doue and Vitinha in PSG's heavy win at the Etihad.

Those errors betrayed a 6ft 5in frame with the manoeuvrability and burst of an 18-wheeler. Donnarumma might still be just 27 years old but his movement in recent months betrays every one of his 12 years as a first-team player, 553 games on the clock and a lot of rubber burned off those tyres.

You could potentially add Antonio Nusa's goal, Leipzig's second equaliser, into the category of shots Donnarumma might have got down to quicker. It's a 0.2 xG shooting position, one that the Norwegian hit fiercely enough that its post-shot value was 0.65. In other words, Donnarumma would have been doing very well if he saved it. This is, however, Manchester City's goalkeeper, one recruited for his shot-stopping above all else. You're entitled to expect him to do very well.

Especially when he was so cataclysmically clumsy for the first equaliser. Any goalkeeper's primary job is to protect his goal. In drifting three yards off his line when Riedle Baku was in a crossing position, Donnarumma was trying to take the easy way out. Again, a shot-stopper who is quicker to get down to the ball might have dealt with it. Certainly the Italian couldn't argue much that he had been unlucky; replays would suggest Baku saw the gap and hit it precisely.

Ridle Baku sneaks one in at the near post past Donnarumma 😤Stream the #UCL on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/tgP6KwASuh

Of course Donnarumma had had his moments earlier, a smart diving save denying Christoph Baumgartner's long-range strike. The same is true of this season and his City career as a whole. At his best, he has recovered that aura of his final months at PSG and across 56 games in the Premier League and Champions League, he has conceded six fewer goals than the post-shot xG value of the shots he has faced. In last season's Premier League he was one of the better pure shot-stoppers in the league; this time he is there or thereabouts.

As a whole, Donnarumma has been fine. It's just that he was not bought to be fine. If you're tolerating a goalkeeper who can't give you much at all in possession, it is because you want the best in the world at keeping the ball out. It seems like a long, long time since Donnarumma could lay claim to that moniker.

While there can be little doubt about Unai Emery’s status as an elite manager in the modern game, matches at the Nou Camp continue to be the stuff of nightmares.

His record at Barcelona now reads 15 defeats from 16 matches and this was another difficult evening with Aston Villa unable to banish the demons for the man who has transformed their club.

It was Emery’s 55th birthday and with the Prince of Wales and Prince George both in attendance, Villa fans were hopeful of another memorable European night. But from the moment midfielder João Gomes handed Barcelona their opening goal, it was always going to be an uphill struggle.

Emery has suffered many uncomfortable occasions at this grand old stadium, none more so than the notorious “La Remontada” of 2017 when he last competed here in the Champions League with Paris St-Germain.

This latest visit would become his heaviest defeat in Europe as Villa manager. With three wins from the opening four matches, they still have a fine chance of progressing to the knockout stage. Yet, aside from the mistakes, there will be a sense that Villa could have capitalised more against a team in the midst of a defensive injury crisis. They did have a number of chances in the first half but were left to rue their lack of ruthlessness.

“In 1982, Villa won the European Cup, and we like to think about playing in this competition again and trying to repeat that success,” Emery said. “Barcelona are favourites for what they have done in the last ten years; now they need to prove why they are favourites.

It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”

#1082. Cristiano Ronaldo retires from the Portugal national team following rift with manager

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's the end of an era: Cristiano Ronaldo, the Portuguese soccer star, announced his decision to retire from the Portuguese national team. Ronaldo, who will turn 42 next year, is considered one of the best players in the history of the sport, and announced his retirement from international soccer after 23 years representing Portugal, winning Euro 2016 and two editions of the UEFA Nations League. Cristiano followed the decision of his long-time rival Lionel Messi, who retired from the Argentine national team last month. Over his career with Portugal, he scored 146 goals in 234 games.

Portugal estará sempre em mim pic.twitter.com/dnFj51rxmh

Ronaldo's decision follows a rift with the current head coach Jorge Jesus. Last month, the striker left Portugal's training camp aboard his private jet following a disagreement with the coach, followed by an open letter and apologies to the fans and the team where he explained his decision, without mentioning the manager. The Portuguese federation later suspended the player for 30 days but he was eligible to be called for the upcoming games against Denmark and Wales.

Ronaldo posted a video message on his social media announcing his decision to retire from the national team: "To the Portuguese people, the day has come to hand back the number seven shirt of the national team that belongs to us all. I never felt it was exclusively mine. But for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and taking it with me to stadiums all over the world. Today the time has come to hand it over to the future. It was not an easy decision, because there are decisions that are not made solely with the head; they are also made with the heart."

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner played his sixth and last World Cup this summer in the United States, Canada and Mexico, when Portugal were eliminated by Spain in the round of 16 of the tournament.

"A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever is coming to an end. When I look back and think of everything I've experienced with the national team, I don't just see matches, goals, records or trophies. I see people. I see immigrants who, for 90 minutes, felt Portugal was a little bit closer. I see millions of Portuguese people whom I've never met in person, but who have been part of my life. Because, at the end of the day, football is so much more than just a game. Football is about the people. Throughout my entire career with the national team, I've strived to push my limits. I wanted to win, I wanted to be the best, I wanted to make history," he said.

"I've always been hard on myself. I've always wanted more; I've always believed we could go further. And I gave everything I had for this shirt. There were perfect afternoons and evenings; there were victories I'll never forget. There were defeats that I still find hard to recall today. I also failed, I also suffered, and there were moments when I wasn't able to give the Portuguese people what they so desperately wanted. But I never gave up. And above all, I never stopped feeling proud to represent Portugal. Over the years, I've learnt some very simple things. Goals come and go, trophies end up in museums, and records are eventually broken. But there is one thing that time can never erase: the place we hold in people's hearts. If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget your worries, and feel nothing but pride in our country, then it was all worth it. Because that's what being Portuguese is all about. We suffer together, we rise together. No captain walks alone and you're all part of my story. Portugal will always need young people who dream, players who never give up, new generations who believe it's possible to reach places no one has reached before. Because a country that continues to create new heroes is a country that never stops believing in itself."

Former Manchester United legend Dimitar Berbatov has blasted his old side, saying they deserve to be in the relegation zone.

United plunged into the bottom three on Saturday afternoon, perversely as neighbours Manchester City lost 3-1 away to Nottingham Forest.

The Bulgarian looked devastated when he was informed of United’s predicament while working on beIN Sports' coverage of the City game but still sounded hopeful that United could turn their form around.

When his attention was drawn to the Premier League table, the two-time Premier League winner initially had his head in his hands before saying: 'I don't believe it, but the way United are playing sometimes they deserve to be there honestly.'

Berbatov then took up a more positive tune saying: ‘Tomorrow they still have a game.'

United host Aston Villa on Sunday and after winning against Roma in midweek have the perfect opportunity finally to end their seven-game winless run in the league.

Berbatov could barely look at the table after United plunged into the drop zone

Berbatov won five major trophies as well as Premier League golden boot in four years at Manhchetser United

The fixture could prove either to be the nail in the coffin for United manager Michael Carrick or afford him more time after a woeful start to the season.

Berbatov won his two Premier Leagues alongside Carrick and will hope his ex-colleague can find a way to keep his job.

If he fails to guide his team to a victory against Villa it could be bleak for Carrick, as he has not been given any guarantees over his future beyond Sunday's game against Aston Villa.

Club chiefs handed Carrick more time to turn the club's season around following the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth a fortnight ago amid speculation he could be replaced by Eddie Howe or Julian Nagelsmann.

In the two games since then, Carrick's side have lost at Chelsea and staged a rousing comeback over Roma in the Champions League to secure a first win in ten games.

But now the onus is on Carrick to build on the momentum gained from their Champions League victory.

#1079. USMNT's Gold Cup path to look different as Concacaf unveils revamped group-stage format

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

For the United States men's national team to win their first Concacaf Gold Cup since 2021, they'll now need to contend with a new format in the 2027 edition. The tournament will run from June 17 through July 11, with major changes coming to the group stage. It will still include only 16 teams, but instead of those teams being split into four groups of four teams each, they'll now be split into only two eight-team groups. Fifteen of those teams will qualify via the Gold Cup preliminary round and join guest nation Saudi Arabia in the tournament.

That shift has the goal of making the group stage more exciting, as not only does it add an extra game due to each team playing four teams instead of three, but it also allows a chance for chaos, as four teams will go through to the knockouts from each group. While the new game is added, that won't change how the knockouts look, as those will proceed as normal.

"The Gold Cup is our region's premier men's national team competition, and we are really excited about what this new format will bring to the tournament's Group Stage," said Concacaf president and FIFA vice president Victor Montagliani. "Our fans want to see the best teams in our region compete against each other, and this format will create more opportunities for those matchups to happen earlier in the competition. At the same time, every match will matter, with teams facing a balanced mix of opponents and competing for a place in the knockout rounds. We believe this will make for a more competitive and exciting Gold Cup from the very first match through to the final."

How matchups are determined is where things get a little confusing, as they will organize the eight teams into ranking bands of two teams each, with a predetermined fixture matrix ensuring that each team plays a balanced schedule of opponents.

This is to prevent a situation where two strong Concacaf sides essentially ensure that others don't have a chance to advance, which could lead to more interesting fixtures in the knockout stages depending on how it goes.

🚨🏆 The rumors are confirmed! Gold Cup will have a whole new format in 2027. @FabrizioRomano breaks it down! pic.twitter.com/ydD1ZwbBvK

For the knockouts, nothing changes from how things used to look, as those four teams advancing from each group will then be placed into a single bracket, with the highest-finishing teams in each group facing off against the lower-finishing teams in the opposite group. There will then be no reseeding as the quarterfinals will determine the semifinal pairings in the road to the championship.

#1078. Liverpool calamity hands Iraola his most chastening night yet

Andoni Iraola looked up to the ceiling of Fenerbahce’s media auditorium as he tried to find the words to describe the madness he had just witnessed.

“Cheap” was his first conclusion, swiftly followed by “messy”; technically, Liverpool’s head coach was right but this was a moment when nobody would have found issue had he gone further. “Absurd” and “preposterous” would have been more accurate portrayals of this calamity.

Liverpool have won two European trophies in Istanbul, but they do not tend to enjoy visits to Turkey. Roy Hodgson, in August 2010, was the last Anfield manager to oversee a win here and there was an irony that the hero of that night in Trabzon – Dirk Kuyt – masterminded this downfall.

Kuyt, interim head coach, got a remarkable response out of a Fenerbahce team who had amassed 1,086 Premier League appearances between them and he was as giddy as the locals after Mason Greenwood, Archie Brown and substitute Vedat Muriqi scored to give the club a famous night.

But even Kuyt would have been the first to recognise the helping hand Fenerbahce were afforded. Liverpool were meek, naïve, and while the Turkish side danced in the rain on the Asian side of the city, Iraola was left to dissect the most chastening 90 minutes of his short Anfield career.

“It’s frustration because it’s a difficult place to come here and to play,” said Iraola. “During most of the game, we were thinking: ‘OK we can win this one.’ But obviously it hasn’t happened. We conceded, I think, messy goals, especially the first and the third one. The second one is a rebound.”

Yet it all started so smoothly. For all that Fenerbahce tried to put Liverpool out of their stride with a soundtrack of high-pitched whistling, Iraola’s side kept the ball well and they might have been ahead in the fifth minute but Victor Muñoz and Bradley Barcola, playing as a central striker, erred.

The first half in Istanbul is brought to an end and we are all square heading into the break. Liverpool took the lead through Nyoni but Greenwood’s deflected free-kick has Fenerbahce on level terms at half-time.

One added minute at the end of this first half.

Greenwood has been Fenerbahce’s best player by far tonight and he tests Alisson. Lukaku finds Greenwood with a pass forward down the left channel and, from inside the Liverpool penalty area, the latter forces Alisson into a decent save.

What started off as an encouraging performance has descended into something ordinary at best for Liverpool. They are being overrun in midfield and the pace of Greenwood down Fenerbahce’s right has the beating of Kostas Tsimikas on every occasion. Andoni Iraola will be delighted to get in for half-time all square - if Liverpool can see it out.

Greenwood has an opportunity from the right side of the box. He tries to beat Alisson at his near post but drags it wide.

Munoz’s cross from near the byline is met by Barcola and the Frenchman’s header goes narrowly wide of the far post.

Tsimikas’ inswinging corner from the right is put into a dangerous area and Skriniar’s header goes over his own bar for another on the other side. Szoboszlai feeds one in towards the near post and Lukaku heads away.

Mason Greenwood is having his name bellowed around the stadium though the deflection off Jeremy Jacquet is the only reason he has scored. Emotions are running high in the stadium, especially in the press box which seems to be an overspill for home supporters. One of Trey Nyoni’s former coaches has an observer’s seat here and he cheered why Nyoni scored. Greenwood’s leveller saw those who had taken umbrage at something so inoffensive return the cheering ten-fold with some pretty colourful gestures, too.

The hosts are back on level terms. Fenerbahce have a free-kick not far outside the Liverpool penalty area, one that should never have been given after Szoboszlai is penalised for a foul on Kante that was not a foul. Greenwood steps up to take and his free-kick takes a huge deflection off Jacquet. That deflection takes it away from Alisson and into the Liverpool net. Alisson is not impressed with his wall.

Fenerbahce are inches away from equalising moments after going behind as they hit the frame of the goal. Brown’s cross from the left side of the box finds Kahveci, whose shot comes back off the bar. It would have been a very close call with offside had the ball gone in.

The visitors take the lead in Istanbul and it is 19-year-old Nyoni who scores. A cross from Szoboszlai into the Fenerbahce penalty area is headed out to the edge of the box, where Nyoni volleys it first time. The shot takes a small deflection off Oppong and beats Ederson.

What a moment for Trey Nyoni 🥹 The young Liverpool midfielder scores his first professional goal, and he does it on the Champions League stage ✨ 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Vtj4Yd3tnn

Fenerbahce want a penalty. The ball is played in behind the Liverpool defence and Greenwood takes a sensational first touch. Tsimikas races back and there is a small push on Greenwood, who goes down. The referee waves the appeals away and the VAR clears the incident.

Should Barcola have done better there? Ngumoha finds Gomez in acres of space out on the right. Gomez then first time delivers a very dangerous cross right through the corridor of uncertainty looking for Barcola but the Frenchman cannot connect.

Munoz wins Liverpool a corner out on the right after Yuksek blocked the cross from the Spaniard. Szoboszlai’s outswinger is headed away at the near post by Yuksek, who has made two good defensive actions in a matter of moments.

Liverpool have so much more quality on the ball when they keep possession but the final ball - especially from the left hand side - is letting them down at the moment. They are making light of a sodden pitch and some overzealous attempts by Fenerbahce to disrupt them. The first 15 minutes has been played out primarily to a soundtrack of high-pitched whistling but, looking at those fans around us, none of them are getting involved. Could it be the whistles are being piped in on a pre-recorded file?

Szoboszlai hits the free-kick but ends up hitting his own man. The effort did appear to be going on target but Munoz got in the way. Liverpool’s plan to set up a mini wall of their own to block out the view of Ederson backfired.

Ngumoha shows great footwork to skip past a few Fenerbahce defenders before Kante barges right into the back of the English teenager to give Liverpool a free-kick not far outside the Fenerbahce penalty area.

Liverpool have dominated possession in these early stages and have settled into the game well. Fenerbahce may not be in the best of form but this is still a tricky away trip.

Liverpool come close to the opening goal of the game. Tsimikas’ cross from the left comes all the way to the back post, where Munoz hits it. The Spaniard scuffs his effort and the ball comes to Barcola, who also scuffs his shot. The ball comes back to Munoz, whose powerful shot is parried behind by Ederson for a corner.

Fenerbahce deal with the initial delivery but Liverpool keep it alive. Szoboszlai sends in a dangerous delivery, which Jacquet meets, but the Frenchman’s header from six yards out goes wide. Jacquet should have done better with that chance.

Before we get going, we pause to pay tribute to Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died the other day.

We are under way in Istanbul, with the weather similar tonight in Turkey as to what it was like in Barcelona last night. Can Liverpool make it four wins from four in this season’s Champions League?

Both sides emerge from the tunnel into the pouring rain and we are moments away from kick-off in Istanbul. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Fenerbahce: Ederson; Semedo, Skriniar, Oppong, Brown; Guendouzi, Kante, Yuksek; Greenwood, Lukaku, Kahveci. Substitutes: Cetin, Akurktoglu, Demir, Muldur, Muriqi, Mercan, Elmaz, Nene, Aydin, Mimovic.

So many of Fenerbahce’s team were Premier League regulars, which begged the question - is this a team with more English top-flight experience than Liverpool? The answer is here: Liverpool’s starting line-up has 1241 Premier League appearances. Fenerbahce have 1086.

“I think we have been [rotating] basically all the season. You play every three, four days you have to refresh the legs. The defensive positions we do not have as many options. We have injuries but offensively I think we can rotate a little bit and today we can see other players.”

On Bradley Barcola playing as a central striker:

“I think Bradley, even Victor [Munoz], are players that are wingers but have played sometimes up front. I think we should be mobile. I think we should attack the spaces that are there. They are there to have good combinations outside. We do not expect them to stay there as the nine. I think Bradley can do this job very well.”

The Hungarian has been struggling of late with a hamstring injury but, having returned to the matchday squad on Sunday against Arsenal, he is now back into the starting XI tonight.

Andoni Iraola says he will not waste any more time thinking about the penalty Liverpool were denied against Arsenal and won’t seek an explanation from Pro Ref. There was a significant fallout following the 1-0 loss at Anfield on Sunday with many judges believing Stuart Attwell, who was VAR, should have consulted match official Andy Madley to highlight an obvious pull by Jurrien Timber that prevented Alexander Isak heading a Bradley Barcola cross.

Liverpool’s head coach explained in the heat of the moment that he would tell his players to go down if they felt contact in the area and Cody Gakpo, the Netherlands international, explained last night in Istanbul it was a message the squad had taken on board.

“As a team, we play pretty fair – maybe we should dive some more like the gaffer said,” Gakpo, who also had claims to be awarded a penalty against Arsenal, explained. “On both occasions you could have given a penalty or a foul, but they decided not. We have to live with the decision. That’s it.”

But as angry as he was with the situation, Iraola has drawn a line on the matter. He is not going to seek out Pro Ref for a discussion – even though he feels a number of decisions have gone against Liverpool this season – and is channelling his energy into other situations.

Iraola said: “I didn’t ask for an explanation and I haven’t received an explanation, no. I told you what you I think about the plays but, honestly, I don’t have the time to [speak to Pro Ref]. I have been preparing for Fenerbahce. It is just two days between games so I have just been focusing on this game and the opposition and how to prepare the team.”

Liverpool have made the long trip to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce on matchday four of the Champions League.

Liverpool enter this fixture having won all three Champions League matches thus far, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal to make it nine points from nine for Andoni Iraola’s side. Liverpool’s five-game unbeaten streak was ended by Arsenal in the league on Sunday. They return to the city where the club enjoyed one of their most memorable nights, beating AC Milan in the Champions League final 21 years ago.

“Istanbul is always going to be very special for Liverpool,” Iraola said. “It is difficult to find a more important night. Tomorrow [tonight] it won’t be easy, you talk about statistics, especially English teams playing here. They have very good players and a very good squad, they know how to play in this competition. We have to start strong in the game. It is very early in the season to establish comparisons. We want to continue how we have done in the Champions League, three games and nine points, it is a good chance to get to 12 points and then finish in the top eight. Champions League away is very difficult.”

In addition to the long-term absentees Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni, both Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong have missed the trip to Turkey.

Fenerbahce have made a slow start to their Champions League campaign, taking just two points from their opening three fixtures. They have drawn twice against Roma and Slavia Prague at home whilst they suffered a heavy 6-0 loss at Aston Villa. Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt has been appointed their interim coach following the resignation of Ismail Kartal following their recent defeat to arch rivals Galatasaray just over a week ago.

“It is a great opportunity for us to show what we can do,” Kuyt said. “It is also a great opportunity for me, a game between two teams that are very important to me. We have a very good plan, and we have to believe in this plan. No-one who loves Fenerbahce is happy with the current situation, but this is a huge opportunity. We have players who have won the Champions League and the World Cup.”

They come into tonight’s match having lost back-to-back league games since drawing against Slavia Prague on matchday three of the Champions League. They have plenty of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Ederson, N’Golo Kante and Romelu Lukaku.

The road to the NWSL Championship in Washington, D.C. will begin this weekend with the start of the playoffs, the league's eight best teams squaring off against each other in the hopes of winning silverware that eludes many of them.

Three previous champions, including 2025 winners, including Gotham FC, who face the Seattle Reign and headline a group that is mostly made up of talented teams hoping to win the NWSL Championship for the first time, are in the field, Gotham enter as the favorites after winning the Shield for the first time, hoping to become the first team to do the double since the Orlando Pride did so in 2024 while aiming to be the first side to win back-to-back championships since the North Carolina Courage did so in 2018 and 2019. The other former winners, the Washington Spirit and the Portland Thorns, meanwhile, meet each other in the quarterfinals on Sunday in one of the most anticipated games of the weekend.

The San Diego Wave are as formidable a contender as any when it comes to the potential first-time champions, the team taking the Shield race to the final day before Gotham picked up their latest accolade. They will take on the Utah Royals, who will make their postseason debut on Friday, while all eyes will shift to the Midwest on Saturday. The Kansas City Current host Angel City in what might be the most competitive matchup of the quarterfinals, the LA-based side most poised to play spoiler after going on a late-season tear fueled by U.S. women's national team hopeful Ally Sentnor.

Here's a look at how the CBS Sports team thinks the NWSL postseason will shake out.

Now that the postseason is here, there is a wave of change. Quite literally. Others chose Gotham FC to follow up a shield win with the NWSL Championship. Kansas City Current has also made the bracket cut to lift the title in the end for one of our analysts.

#1074. Gyokeres the creator and executioner to see nervous Arsenal past Slavia Prague

With a stylish assist and a gorgeous goal, Viktor Gyokeres produced the sort of match-winning performance that suggests the Swedish striker is making significant progress at last. It has not always been straightforward for him at Arsenal, but this was unquestionably one of his better showings, and it continued an encouraging upturn in his form.

Gyokeres has been the second-choice striker for most of this season, with Mikel Arteta usually preferring the more subtle Kai Havertz in attack. There are signs, though, that Gyokeres is now growing in belief. Following this victory over Slavia Prague, which was much more narrow and nervy than it should have been, he has now scored two goals and registered three assists in his last five appearances.

Even more promising than those statistics was his all-round play in Prague. In the first half especially, Gyokeres held on to long passes, combined with his team-mates and tested the opposition with his runs in behind. For Arsenal’s first goal, he found Noni Madueke with a brilliant pass. For their second, he curled a fabulous strike into the top corner.

What a finish from Viktor Gyökeres from a tight angle 📐🎯 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/EET5P7aJ2X

“Really good,” said Arteta of Gyokeres. “Not only the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s great news, because I think he needed that performance.”

Those two moments in the first half eventually ensured another European victory for Arteta’s side, but the manager was far from impressed with the second-half showing. So smooth at first, Arsenal became remarkably ragged by the end. Slavia were deserving of their goal, scored by Wiktor Nowak. It looked like complacency had infected the minds of the Arsenal players, and you could feel Arteta’s fury radiating from the touchline.

“We scored two goals and it should have been three, four or five,” said Arteta. “And at half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning of the second half, we were extremely far from our standards in everything that we have to do, in every basic, in every concept, and in everything we discussed. So much to improve and I take full responsibility for that.”

Without Gabriel Magalhães and David Raya, who both made dramatic stops on the goal-line, this could have become an ugly night for Arsenal against one of the weaker teams in the Champions League. The Czech side have now gone 23 games without a victory in Europe’s premier competition, which equals the longest winless run in European Cup history.

It was a remarkable coincidence that this game fell on November 4, the exact date as the same fixture last season. On that occasion Arsenal were comfortable 3-0 winners, with Mikel Merino scoring twice, and they seemed to be heading towards a similar night when Madueke scored the early opener.

The goal was made by Gyokeres, who held off a defender and then hooked an excellent pass into Madueke’s path. The Arsenal winger had already established his dominance over Oskar Kubiak, his opposite number, and he reached fifth gear before the Polish defender had even reached second. Madueke then slid his finish beneath the body of Nazar Domchak, Slavia’s teenage goalkeeper.

Just as Gyokeres is finding his form, so is Madueke. The absence of the injured Bukayo Saka has given Madueke a run in the side and he seems to be benefiting from it, even if he still lacks the same consistency in decision-making as his England team-mate.

One of Slavia’s many problems in a one-sided first half was their inability to cope with Arsenal’s rotations in midfield. Declan Rice, Martín Zubimendi and Merino were all alternating positions at will, taking turns to drop deep and push forward. Merino could have scored a couple, before he combined sharply with Gyokeres for Arsenal’s second.

Gyokeres has never been the most delicate link-up player, and there have been too many times when the ball has simply bounced off him, but here he was impressively sleek. A quick exchange of passes with Merino allowed him a sight of goal, and the curled finish was sumptuous. For a man known for his power, this was an uncharacteristic demonstration of finesse.

Game over? Arsenal clearly thought so. They certainly came out for the second half like a team that believed the job was done. Arteta became increasingly irate in the first few minutes after the restart, with Ben White on the receiving end of one verbal slap. Rice also received a telling-off, and a yellow card, from the referee after kicking the ball away in annoyance.

Would Slavia have secured a draw if they had been at full strength? They had been weakened by the banishment of their star striker from the club because of a series of disciplinary failings. Tomás Chory, the top scorer for the past two seasons, was chucked out of the team after showing his middle finger to the referee in a recent game. This sort of sanction would have earned Arteta’s approval, no doubt, but it did not increase Slavia’s chances of hurting the Premier League champions in those edgy final few minutes.

Perhaps they will reflect on that decision differently now, given the uncharacteristically wobbly second-half performance by Arsenal. The visitors were vulnerable in the latter stages, when they lacked the control and composure that Arteta expects. Gabriel, too, appeared dismayed by what he was seeing. At one point, he put his hands on his hips and scowled at his team-mates like an angry teacher.

With only a few minutes remaining, Nowak converted a left-wing cross to plunge Arsenal into a proper panic. It required a backs-to-the-wall defensive action, similar to the victory against Liverpool on Sunday, to get over the line.

Always we need to value winning away in the Champions League. It is extremely difficult. Two very different halves. We should have had three or four goals in the first half but we didn’t do it. Right at the start of the second half we were on the back foot, very sloppy and gave balls away. Then we had to suffer. A lot to learn.

We should have scored more in the first half and if we didn’t do that we had to go and do that in the second half.

We made six changes but we know the quality of the players we have. Whether we were lacking something I don’t know but I would have done the same thing [again].

I value what the team has done now, it is 11 away games we played, but our standards should be higher.

Arteta on Gyokeres: "He was really good. A game we believed was good for him, for the spaces he could use. He was really connected to the team. Great news because I think he needed that. Really pleased."

Arteta: "Two very different halves. The first we played at a really high level. At half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning we were extremely far from our standards. Very far from the standards we expect from each other."

First half we played really, really well. We created a lot of chances and could have scored more but the second half was completely different. They stepped up a gear and made it difficult for us and we have to learn from it. Delighted with the win but a lot of things to improve going forward.

Maybe they started pressing a bit higher with more intensity. We had too many giveaways especially in the final third. There was too much running from box to box and we have to manage those reactions and go for the third and fourth goal.

At the end of the day it is three points.

Slavia Prague managed just one shot on goal in the first half worth 0.12 xG but finished the game with 18 shots on Arsenal’s goal and 2.23 xG. Arsenal could easily have dropped points on the balance of the second 45 minutes.

Quite surprised Declan Rice stayed on the pitch for the full 90 minutes there. He seemed to be in a bit of discomfort after a couple of long sprints. And then he got the silly yellow. Arteta perhaps panicking about the result.

A top-two finish means home second legs all the way, and avoidance of the league phase winners until the final.

Arsenal put another win on the board in the Champions League, but what looked like being a cakewalk at half-time was anything but. Arteta will use that second 45 minutes to demonstrate the dangers of not starting a half with full intensity, once Slavia were in top it was hard to wrestle back control.

Arsenal were second best in midfield, it was strange that Lewis-Skelly and Guimaraes stayed on the bench, but they stumbled over the line.

Rice with a chance to pick out Madueke on the counter but his diagonal pass was cut out. Slavia have been sent out with a flea in their ear, and have been much improved so far. Arteta will want Arsenal to stay serious and weather this spell.

Slavia Prague XI: Domchak, Holes, Zima, Vlcek, Suleiman, Moses, Sadilek, Kubiak, Ayaosi, Sturm, Nowak

Subs: Markovic, Rezek, Chaloupek, N’Guessan, Chytil, Provod, Diakite, Kacor, Jurasek, Konecny, Barcot, Kotrba

Good evening from a chilly Prague, where Arsenal are looking for a repeat of the 3-0 victory they secured here exactly one year ago. It’s a remarkable coincidence that Mikel Arteta’s team have travelled to face Slavia Prague on November 4th in back-to-back years.

On that occasion last year, Max Dowman became the youngest player in Champions League history. He should get more minutes tonight from the bench, given that he is currently suspended from Premier League action following his controversial red card against Fleetwood last week.

That’s the most Arteta has rotated between a Premier League and Champions League game so far this season. Telling perhaps that Konsa, Gabriel and Rice – the team’s defensive bedrock – stay in place. But changes on both sides at full-back, and in the attacking midfield areas.

Arsenal XI: Raya; White, Konsa, Gabriel, Hincapie; Rice, Zubimendi, Merino; Madueke, Gyokeres, Eze

Subs: Kepa, Meslier, Saliba, Mosquera, Timber, Calafiori, Lewis-Skelly, Odegaard, Guimaraes, Tzolis, Dowman, Havertz

Arsenal’s critics will still grumble about the style of victory, but, of all clubs, this is a team who have no obligation to play in a way that neutrals might enjoy. Arsenal spent so much of Arsene Wenger’s 22-year reign playing football that was mostly stylish but only sometimes effective in big games. Now they are mostly effective but only occasionally stylish on such occasions. If you asked all the travelling fans at Anfield which they prefer, you would receive an overwhelming response.

David Raya has kept a clean sheet in 54% of his Champions League starts (21 clean sheets from 39 starts), the best ratio of any goalkeeper to start at least 25 games in the competition. 🤯🇪🇸 https://t.co/A1Zpn8kJN9

Arsenal return to Slavia Prague for the third time under Mikel Arteta knowing that three points will be another step towards a top-eight finish in the Champions League league phase.

Arteta’s team were 4-0 winners in the Czech capital in a 2021 Europa League quarter-final second leg, and 3-0 victors at this stage of the Champions League a year ago. Bukayo Saka opened the scoring with a penalty before two second-half goals from Mikel Merino.

Paris-St Germain are top of the table on 12 points after their rout against Villarreal last night. Real Madrid, Liverpool and Real Betis are the three teams who have the chance to join them on maximum points. Arsenal will jump to 10 points with a win, above Bayern Munich, Sporting and Aston Villa at a minimum.

Slavia Prague are top of the Czech league and unbeaten after 13 games this season, but they are winless in the Champions League after fixtures against Lens, Sabah and Fernerbahce.

The fixture should be a presentable opportunity for Arteta to rotate his team, especially after a physically taxing game at Anfield where Arsenal showed their mettle to win at Liverpool’s home for the first time since 2012.

Arsenal’s second-string is very strong, though they did not cover themselves in glory at Fleetwood in the League Cup last week when Max Dowman was sent off. Given the 16-year-old is banned for another two Premier League games, and the attention Arteta’s touchline reaction to the red card attracted, one wonders if he might want to seize a chance to put Dowman back on the horse.

William Saliba’s return to full training is very welcome news, despite Ezri Konsa impressing in his absence. Saliba travelled with the squad to Prague, and could make his first appearance of the season following a back injury which flared up in France’s World Cup semi-final against Spain. With fixtures against Manchester City, Borussia Dortmund, Brentford, Spurs, Real Madrid, Bournemouth and Manchester United before the end of 2026 though, they will not want rush him.

Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze are other players pushing for greater involvement from the start of matches.

#1073. Steve Cherundolo names first U.S. U-23 roster on road to 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The road to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics is underway as Steve Cherundolo's roster for games against Scotland and Ukraine has been named, and it's an experienced group of players. Six players on this roster have been called up to the United States men's national team, and four earned caps during the recent September/October international break, while Parma's Benjamin Cremaschi was a member of the 2024 Olympic squad and is eligible to still be involved in the 2028 edition of the tournament.

Looking at the experience with eight players being based abroad and so many being on the fringes of the senior side, it shows just how deep the talent available to Cherundolo is for the Olympics during what is an exciting time for U.S. Soccer.

"We're very excited to bring this talented and polished group of players together and begin our journey toward the 2028 Olympic Games," Cherundolo said. "We're eager to get to work, establish our identity and build a strong foundation for what lies ahead. Our first international matches will be a great opportunity to challenge ourselves, compete, and grow together as a team."

They'll begin training for this camp alongside the senior team at the Arthur M. Blank National Training Center, similarly to how the United States women's national team set up their last camp. Not only does it showcase a synergy between the two sides, but it also provides both Cherundolo and Mauricio Pochettino with opportunities to oversee each squad, because when they're called next, considering how young the senior team is, too, there could be shifts between the two squads.

It's an important camp as it's Cherundolo's first since taking over the U-23s, so we'll get our first look at how the United States youth stacks up under him against solid opponents from around the world. Given the experience that's available to him and how tight competition will be for the Olympics, as three overage players can go in the 23-man squad for the competition, everyone will need to be on their game immediately.

#1071. Liga MX title race tightens as Club America stumble down the stretch

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Two matchdays remain in the Apertura portion of the Liga MX season, and there's everything to play for, from the title down to the final playoff spots. CBS Sports Golazo Network will be the place to see plenty of the key action. Club America lead Chivas Guadalajara and Cruz Azul only on goal difference, while Atlas are also a surprise contender for the title, trailing by only two points. Club America may have the best attack in the league, with Henry Martin leading the line and getting back to his best, but a potentially tricky matchup with Pumas could cost them points.

Club America have lost only twice this season, but they have scuffled a bit and are winless in their last three, including a loss to Pachuca, who are led by the league's top scorer in the ageless Salomon Rondon. At the opposite end of the spectrum, the final four playoff spots are essentially up for grabs, as anyone currently fifth to 11th could be passed, and only four teams have been mathematically eliminated from playoff contention.

Technically, Puebla are done if anyone on 22 points secures a point, but even the fact that they have a chance in 14th place shows how competitive this season has been. But it's also one that could bring quite a shock if the table ends as it is currently, with Monterrey on the outside looking in at the playoffs.

Date: Saturday, Nov. 7 | Time: 8 p.m. ETLocation: Estadio Nemesio Diez -- Toluca de Lerdo, MexicoLive stream: CBS Sports Golazo NetworkOdds: Toluca -170; Draw +340; Monterrey +360

Traveling away to face Toluca, Rayados need all the points that they can get and then some. They haven't missed the playoffs since 2016, and despite being the third-highest-spending team, behind Atlas and Club America, there hasn't been much to show for it as Matias Almeyda's chaotic management follows the squad through the season. They have talent in the squad, but it's not all coming together all at once. This team is just as likely to win 4-2 as it is to lose by the same score, and that comes down to management, not talent.

On talent, there's no reason for Monterrey to miss the playoffs, and having three of the top 15 scorers on their team shows that this is an attack to be feared. It's anyone's guess if they'll actually get things together in time, but if it doesn't happen Saturday night, only 90 minutes will remain before missing the playoffs becomes reality for the club.

#1068. Clearing the way for a transformative stem-cell treatment for Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Joohi Jimenez-Shahed studies movement disorders, neuromodulation and brain circuit therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Big improvements in Parkinson’s disease treatment have been few and far between. The tantalizing prospect of regenerative stem-cell therapies to address this neurodegenerative condition is therefore creating considerable excitement.

A core component of Parkinson’s is the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, which normally provide carefully controlled neurotransmitter signals to the brain’s movement circuits1. This leads to people having substantial difficulties performing routine activities.

A dopamine-replacement approach provided one of the first major advances in Parkinson’s treatment2. Levodopa, a chemical precursor to dopamine that was introduced in the 1960s, treats symptoms effectively. But the levodopa honeymoon can be short. As the effect duration of each dose wanes, extra doses or medications are required to keep dopamine levels from falling. And the drug can come with a complication that many patients dread — writhing, uncontrolled involuntary movements known as dyskinesia. A surgical approach called deep brain stimulation (DBS) can mitigate these complications effectively3.

The downsides of levodopa raise a question: rather than replacing dopamine, why not replace the cellular machinery that produces it? Enter the dopaminergic stem cell. Engineered from cells sampled from an adult’s own tissues (known as autologous) or from a different individual (allogeneic), induced-pluripotent stem cells can be safely transplanted into human brains and can improve movement-related Parkinson’s symptoms, such as tremors, stiffness and slowness, without worsening dyskinesia4.

Only a few dozen people have received this experimental treatment. Major brain surgery is required to transplant the cells. Allogeneic cell transplants also require recipients to undertake a year of immunosuppression to ensure that the cells survive. Autologous cell transplants avoid this, but it takes 6–8 months to produce the cells for each patient.

It is not yet known how cell therapies will measure up to current standards of care. Early studies have been in people with advanced disease. At this stage, the chance of benefit might be reduced: the cells are implanted into an already degenerating circuit that could be difficult to restore.

Critics might therefore argue that dopamine cell therapies cannot produce a more robust effect than levodopa or DBS without imposing excess cost or risk. But the way that Parkinson’s treatments are investigated and approved can neither fully support this pessimistic view nor provide sufficient evidence for a more optimistic one.

Therapeutic development for Parkinson’s has mainly aimed to relieve symptoms. A more ambitious goal would be to slow the disease’s progression by altering its underlying biology. Yet there are substantial obstacles to developing such a treatment.

Implicit to the concept of disease modification is the need for a biomarker that measures the underlying biological processes5. Although a biological definition of Parkinson’s is emerging, it applies mainly to the identification of early disease. Relatively little is known about how such markers evolve in Parkinson’s, or how they relate to clinical progression6.

Long-term, multi-site observational studies such as the Parkinson’s Precision Medicine Initiative (see go.nature.com/4ayapbI) provide an ideal framework for exploring digital, biological and imaging markers, while benchmarking disease progression. Their success depends on building and sustaining large consortia, and on a healthy dose of time and effort from researchers and study participants, but the studies are constrained by funding inequities.

Even if such biomarkers were already at researchers’ disposal, there is no specific guidance from the US Food and Drug Administration on developing disease-modifying treatments7. The agency’s Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy designation speeds up cell- and gene-therapy development and approval. But eligibility requires only the intent to treat, modify, reverse or cure a serious disorder. As a result, clinical trials of regenerative therapies are likely to be designed to show benefits to a person’s symptoms without incurring the added cost and burden of showing a change in biology — a pragmatic but less ambitious path.

Crucially, supportive evidence for the broader potential of dopaminergic cell therapies is what will define their advantage. Cell dose, optimal treatment timing and objective evidence of cell survival, engraftment and effects on brain-network function would demonstrate whether cell therapies can produce lasting change in people with Parkinson’s. Public–private research partnerships could refine the required measurement tools and generate such data.

The ability to transform stem cells into dopamine-producing neurons and transplant them safely into human brains is momentous. Its use as a treatment extends an opportunity to chart another course for people with Parkinson’s by limiting levodopa complications and possibly the need for DBS. This outcome would bolster the hopes of people with this condition. But the real therapeutic breakthrough will occur only when scientists and regulators converge to advance the goal of restoring neural circuitry and function. That would be a truly bold step towards conquering this this relentless disease.

Manchester City surely cannot win the Champions League with a defence leaking goals and a goalkeeper making errors. But when Erling Haaland is in the team, anything seems possible.

This thrilling victory for City perfectly sums up their season: needless goals conceded, Gianluigi Donnarumma making a mistake, followed by Haaland saving the day with a winning goal.

“How can you stop Haaland?” read the headline in the local Volkszeitung newspaper on the morning of this Champions League clash. The answer is that it has been impossible for RB Leipzig.

Leipzig roll out the Red Bull carpet when they face the Norweigan. He has now scored 13 goals against them in nine matches, the most he has scored against a single team during his career. Enzo Maresca gave him the armband here and his winning goal masked more worries for the City head coach in his back line.

“Keeping the ball, when to keep it, when to go, working together offensively and defensively – you can always be better and there’s always a new chance.”

Haaland had the final say in a match where City were gifted the lead through Castello Lukeba’s own goal, before Donnarumma was exposed at his near post by Ridle Baku’s cheeky finish when the City goalkeeper was positioned for a cross.

This was a victory to bounce back from losing in the Premier League at the weekend, but the question will be how can City mount a title challenge with such a brittle defence. Champions League winners do not leave themselves open at the back like this, and City have now gone seven games without a clean sheet.

#1064. Chasing dynasty: How Gotham FC's NWSL Shield win completes transformation ahead of playoffs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

En route to their second NWSL championship in two years, relatively new Gotham FC recruit Jaedyn Shaw was uninterested in the narratives that underestimated her team. The surprise win at the NWSL Shield-winning Kansas City Current in the playoff quarterfinals was not a surprise to her, and she made it clear with three quick words: "Underdog, my ass."

Shaw had a point on that cold day in the Midwest, and almost exactly a year later, it still stands. Gotham are the NWSL's new dynasty, and their Shield win marked their fifth major title in three years, with a sixth in their sights as the playoffs begin this weekend. The transformation was rapid for a team that has historically been a bottom-dweller, so much so that their 2023 championship triumph was a genuine surprise. They quickly built a title-winning team and reaped the rewards just as swiftly, but even as the muscle memory of title charges returns, Gotham will go about their next NWSL playoff journey differently. The target is officially on their backs, the onus officially on them to live up to the billing.

Gotham have played the vast majority of their playoff games as the lowest-seeded team in the postseason, winning the championship twice in those circumstances. Sunday's quarterfinal against the Seattle Reign, though, will be the first game they play as the unquestionable favorites to win the whole thing. How Gotham will play with the weight of expectations is entirely unclear, since they have never done it before, but it is a good problem of their own creation, one they have chased since the 2023 triumph.

Date: Sunday, Nov. 8 | Time: 12:30 p.m. ETLocation: Sports Illustrated Stadium -- Harrison, N.J.TV: ABC | Live stream: ESPN AppOdds: Gotham FC -150; Draw +265; Seattle Reign +340

Their blitz in the free-agent market in the winter of 2024 laid the foundation for their dynastic run, but the most fascinating feature of Gotham's years-long run of success is the evolution they have undergone since. U.S. women's national team defender Tierna Davidson has become the team's captain, her progressive passing ability making her a key fixture in head coach Juan Carlos Amoros' system. Her club and country teammate Rose Lavelle has become a standout, but the star of the show has been Shaw, who has barely missed a beat since her arrival in September 2025.

Shaw has 14 goals and seven assists in 35 NWSL games with Gotham, her wide-ranging skill set fully on display in Amoros' team. She has been a little bit of everything for the team's attack, which is arguably too reliant on her talents, but it is almost hard to fault Amoros for the approach. The system has allowed Shaw to flourish, in particular bringing out a clear goal-scoring quality that is key to a Gotham team that values defensive work rate first.

"First, I think the commitment they have to defend and the commitment they have to work hard for the team despite being some of the best players technically in the planet," Amoros said about both Shaw and Lavelle after a win over the Chicago Stars in September. "I think that helps the connection, not only between them two. There is a mutual respect there because of that but then also from the whole team. When you have to play and those are the players that produce the chances for us in the final third but then the people that [are] behind them are always supportive of them because of the work they put in and then we try to work a lot with them to how we can find them and how they can connect more with each other and the same with Sam [Kerr]."

He has found a unique way to make Shaw and Lavelle work together, despite the fact that they appear to have overlapping skill sets when it comes time for USWNT head coach Emma Hayes to slot them into her lineup. The pair often play just behind Kerr, an out-and-out striker, and assume the role of strikers themselves while balancing their creative tendencies. They have filled in some gaps along the way -- Kerr, for example, ranks third in the league with 9.67 expected goals since returning to the NWSL on July 16 but has scored just four times. Kerr does, though, have four assists in 17 games, one fewer than Shaw and one more than Lavelle over that span.

The connection between Lavelle and Shaw has offered Gotham a level of dynamism that has been missing in their attack at times over the years, even as they racked up title after title. It helps that the two have enjoyed working alongside each other, the 21-year-old Shaw in particular taking inspiration from Lavelle, a decade her senior.

"I think her movement is some of the best in the world, honestly," Shaw said after that September win over the Stars. "She's able to make stretch runs, drag players. She attracts so many players, opening up space for other players to get on the ball and then getting on the second one, I think, is one of her strengths and is something I'm trying to replicate off of her. I think she's just incredibly smart in soccer knowledge."

For each of them, a return to fitness after small injuries in the final weeks of the regular season comes not a moment too soon. Kerr's inconsistency is not the only attacking issue they will need to overcome -- Jordyn Dudley will miss the postseason with a foot fracture she sustained last month, her impressive rookie season coming to a close with four goals and three assists. Lavelle and Shaw will be particularly useful against the Reign, whose defensive qualities continue to be a strength.

Shaw has become the focal point of Gotham's reinvention in recent years, but Amoros' side has added experienced options in a wide variety of positions since the 2023 championship. The vast majority of Gotham's likely starters on Sunday will have joined the club after the 2023 playoff run, a steady stream of important players signing themselves up since. Ann-Katrin Berger, the 2024 goalkeeper of the year, made the move not long after Davidson and Lavelle did, and European champion Jess Carter followed right after. Midfielder Jaelin Howell, who has been in and around the USWNT, was recruited in time for the 2025 season, and Shaw joined months later. Left back Guro Reiten has two goals and six assists since making her club debut in April, while Kerr made the move at roughly the same time as midfielder Denise O'Sullivan, a two-time NWSL champion with the North Carolina Courage.

Gotham's reinvention is constant, the core evolving each and every season. It is a unique route to the top, but in another season of change, they found the consistency they have been chasing since the 2023 championship. The underdog label has well and truly been shed, the team chasing another tag entirely -- a third championship would put them level with the Portland Thorns as the most successful team in the league's history.
